summary: In her wrongful-dismissal lawsuit, former AHS CEO Athana Mentzelopoulos alleges that after she was fired on Jan 8, 2025, Andre Tremblay, who replaced her as interim CEO, ordered staff to cancel a meeting that week with the Auditor General about AHS's forensic audit and internal procurement review (CBC). name: AIMCo board of directors removed and replaced (Nov 2024)
summary: By O.C. 298/2024 (Nov 7, 2024) the Alberta cabinet rescinded the appointments of all 10 AIMCo directors and appointed Finance Minister Nate Horner a member and designated him chair of the board (O.C. 298/2024; CBC: the board's "sole director and chair"); by O.C. 318/2024 (Nov 20, 2024) it rescinded Horner and appointed Stephen Harper chair, reappointing three former directors (per the King's Printer orders). CBC reported CEO Evan Siddall and three other executives were also out.

name: Alberta Office of the Election Commissioner dissolved (Bill 22, Nov 2019)
summary: Bill 22, the Reform of Agencies, Boards and Commissions and Government Enterprises Act, ended Election Commissioner Lorne Gibson's contract (to run to 2023) and moved the role into the Office of the Chief Electoral Officer; Elections Alberta said the office was dissolved Nov 22, 2019. Gibson had levied more than $200,000 in fines in his investigation of the 2017 UCP leadership race (CBC, Global). The Bill was introduced by Finance Minister Travis Toews; the Opposition called it "corrupt" (Edmonton Journal).

name: Public Inquiry into Anti-Alberta Energy Campaigns report delayed four times (2020-21)
summary: Steve Allan's inquiry had a July 2020 deadline and a $2.5M budget; cabinet extended it four times (to July 30, 2021) and raised the budget to $3.5M (Global). Justice Karen Horner dismissed Ecojustice's challenge.

name: Alberta NDP Leader's Gala with leader Naheed Nenshi, Calgary (Nov 28, 2025)
summary: Alberta NDP leader Naheed Nenshi's LinkedIn post says the party's first Leader's Gala was "a resounding success" with a sold-out room in Calgary; attendee posts date it to Nov 28, 2025. The Nurse Practitioner Association of Alberta posted that its vice-president attended. The party's event page (albertandp.ca/leader-s-gala) now returns 404 and no Wayback capture was found, so the ticket price is unknown.

name: Alberta Bill 14 ends the court reference on the independence referendum question (Dec 2025)
summary: Chief electoral officer Gordon McClure referred the proposed independence question to the Court of King's Bench. Bill 14, tabled Dec 4, 2025 by Justice Minister Mickey Amery, would end that proceeding; Justice Colin Feasby ruled Dec 5 that the proposal would be unconstitutional (CBC). Bill 14 then passed, removing constitutional vetting and the CEO's power to refer; CBC says it made the ruling moot.

name: Bal des lumières mental-health gala, $1.43M raised, Montreal (Mar 23, 2016)
summary: A Bell Canada news release says the second Bal des lumières, held at the Bell Centre on Mar 23, 2016, raised $1,430,000 for three Montreal mental-health foundations, with more than 850 guests including Health Minister Gaétan Barrette, Transport Minister Jacques Daoust and Montreal Mayor Denis Coderre, who is quoted. The release says the ball was co-chaired by George Cope (Bell), Serge Godin (CGI), Geoff Molson (Club de hockey Canadien/Bell Centre/evenko) and Louis Vachon (National Bank).

name: BC Liberal $5,000-a-plate fundraiser dinner with Premier Christy Clark, Mission Hill Winery, West Kelowna (Jan 26, 2017)
summary: Premier Christy Clark attended a BC Liberal fundraiser dinner at Mission Hill Winery on Jan 26, 2017 at $5,000 per plate; Global News reported 20 guests and the Globe reported 12 contributing guests per the BC Liberals. Clark defended the event the next morning at a Greater Westside Board of Trade breakfast. Kelowna Capital News reported it was organized by Agriculture Minister Norm Letnick.

name: Private BC Liberal fundraising dinner with Premier Christy Clark and Minister Rich Coleman, Vancouver (Feb 23, 2016): over $1 million raised
summary: theBreaker reports that a private BC Liberal fundraising dinner coordinated by Patrick Kinsella was held in Vancouver on Feb 23, 2016, with Premier Christy Clark and Housing Minister and Deputy Premier Rich Coleman as special guests, raising more than $1 million. It links the dinner to Feb 26, 2016 donations, including $200,000 and $100,000 from Peter Wall companies, $100,000 from Bruno Wall's company, and $200,000 from John Redekop Construction plus $100,000 from Peter Redekop.

Ticket price and amount raised not stated in this source.

name: BC NDP $700 invitation-only breakfast with Housing Minister Ravi Kahlon for candidate Ravi Parmar, Langford (May 17, 2023)
summary: Black Press reported a $700 invitation-only breakfast fundraiser on May 17, 2023 featuring B.C. Housing Minister Ravi Kahlon in support of NDP by-election candidate Ravi Parmar (Langford-Juan de Fuca). An email advertising it bore the signature of Keycorp Developments, and promised attendees would hear about the Homes for People plan; cheques were to be payable to 'BC NDP'. BC Green House Leader Adam Olsen called it 'a cash-for-access exclusive event designed for developers'. The NDP said ticketed fundraisers are legal and invitations went to a wide range of people.

name: BC NDP 'evening gala' with Premier David Eby and caucus, Surrey – postponed (scheduled Feb 4, 2024)
summary: CityNews reported the BC NDP postponed a fundraiser billed as an 'evening gala' with Premier David Eby and the NDP caucus, set for the evening of Sunday Feb 4, 2024 in Surrey, after multiple groups announced protests. Party spokesperson Heather Libby cited timing. Ticket sales were to fund NDP candidates' campaigns in Surrey. Event did not take place on that date.

name: CSIS overseas operation halted mid-course, then resumed after delay (2022)
summary: NSIRA found that the decision to halt an active CSIS operation abroad was not made by the CSIS Director, that there was no written record of a direction from the Minister, and that the halt "created unnecessary danger for the CSIS team"; the operation proceeded after a delay (NSIRA; CBC). NSIRA does not name who halted it. CBC reported that in Sept 2022 then-Public Safety Minister Marco Mendicino asked NSIRA to review the episode.

name: CSIS threat-reduction measure against Indian intelligence networks scaled down (2017)
summary: Per NSICOP's classified 2019 draft as quoted by The Bureau (inquiry exhibit TSC0000014): CSIS planned a 2017 threat-reduction measure against two alleged Indian intelligence networks but "scaled down its intervention on advice from Privy Council Office and Public Safety", did not engage elected officials or journalists as planned, and took no action on the Vancouver network; Global Affairs did not raise the diplomat's activities because of preparations for the Prime Minister's India trip.

name: CSIS warrant application held 54 days in the Public Safety minister's office (2021)
summary: The foreign interference inquiry heard that a CSIS warrant application sat in then-Public Safety Minister Bill Blair's office for 54 days after it went to his chief of staff Zita Astravas; Blair testified he signed it the day he first saw it (CBC). The Bureau reported the warrant concerned former Ontario minister Michael Chan and that Democracy Watch would file a conflict complaint.

name: CTCCO event for the 70th anniversary of the founding of the People's Republic of China, Toronto area (Sept 29, 2019), attended by the PRC consul general
summary: The Epoch Times reports that the Confederation of Toronto Chinese Canadian Organizations (CTCCO), whose president is Weng Guoning, organized an event in the Toronto area on Sept 29, 2019 to mark the PRC's 70th anniversary, and that PRC Consul General Han Tao attended. It names as attendees federal Small Business Minister Mary Ng, Liberal MP Geng Tan, Ontario PC MPPs Vincent Ke and Aris Babikian (who presented congratulatory proclamations), and city councillors Jim Karygiannis (Toronto) and Isa Lee (Markham). It also says MPP Billy Pang sent a representative.

name: Concurrent immigration powers
summary: Section 95 establishes concurrent provincial and federal immigration lawmaking, with federal law prevailing on repugnancy; s.91(25) assigns naturalization and aliens federally.

name: First post-Confederation Immigration Act
summary: Establishes immigration offices, agents and quarantine arrangements and passenger duties; wider passenger protection provisions are described in the museum history.

name: Chinese immigration head-tax statute
summary: Creates an entry duty of $50, subject to exemptions; imposes a vessel limit of one covered immigrant per fifty tons.

name: Royal Commission report catalogue
summary: Official catalogue identifies the 1885 report and commissioners Joseph Adolphe Chapleau and John Hamilton Gray; seven digitized report parts are linked.

name: Chinese Immigration Act amendment
summary: Amends R.S.C. c.67: adds exemptions tied to marriage and railway transit and allocates one-quarter of collected duties and revenues to the collecting province.

name: Departure-registration amendment
summary: Replaces departure/re-entry registration provision; requires written notice and a one-dollar fee and provides a return/refund mechanism within six months.

name: Chinese Immigration Act, 1900
summary: Replacement statute sets a $100 entry duty with exceptions; s.2 defers commencement to 1901-01-01; s.3 lists repealed enactments.

name: Chinese Immigration Act, 1900 takes effect
summary: Statutory commencement date for the 1900 replacement law and its repeal provisions; not the assent date.

name: Immigration inquiry established
summary: LAC describes establishment of the inquiry, its mandate, commissioners and surviving reports/hearing transcripts.

name: Chinese Immigration Act, 1903
summary: Replacement statute sets a $500 entry duty with exceptions; s.2 defers commencement to 1904-01-01; s.3 lists repealed enactments.

name: Chinese Immigration Act, 1903 takes effect
summary: Statutory commencement date for the 1903 replacement law and its repeal provisions; not the assent date.

name: Immigration Act replacement
summary: Act uses the short title The Immigration Act and defines immigrant, agent and landing; wider exclusion/deportation provisions need section-by-section extraction.

name: Continuous-journey enabling amendment
summary: Replaces s.30(1) of R.S.C. 1906 c.93, authorizing prohibition by proclamation or order for arrivals other than continuous journey with through tickets.

name: Continuous-journey order approved
summary: LAC catalogue dates this order introduced April 23, considered May 11 and approved May 27, 1908; points to P.C.1908-0919.

name: Immigration Act, 1910
summary: Replaces general immigration framework; opening text defines the minister as Minister of the Interior and introduces three-year domicile provisions.

name: Racially exclusionary order approved; enforcement not established
summary: LAC records approval August 12 following introduction June 2 and consideration August 10. Museum reproduces the exclusionary language and says it does not appear to have been officially invoked.

name: Immigration Act amendment; domicile extended
summary: Amends minister definition to Minister of Immigration and Colonization; changes domicile qualifying residence from three to five years, subject to specified exceptions.

name: Chinese Immigration Act, 1923 receives assent
summary: Narrowly confines entry to specified classes and repeals earlier Chinese immigration enactments in s.43. Statute heading says June 30, not July 1.

name: Exclusion regime begins
summary: Parks Canada identifies July 1 as the beginning of exclusion; keep separate from June 30 royal assent verified in statute scan.

name: Chinese Immigration Act repealed
summary: Original c.19 assented May14,1947; s.4 expressly repeals the Chinese Immigration Act, R.S.C.1927 c.95. Sections1–3 also amend transit bonds, repeal s.80 and legislate service-dependant admission. Assent and repeal provision are verified; no separate commencement proclamation found or assumed.

name: Immigration Act, 1952
summary: New general Immigration Act; opening definitions identify the Director of Immigration Branch and distinguish entry, admission and deportation.

name: Part I immigration regulations replaced
summary: Order revokes P.C.1954-1351 as amended and substitutes Part I regulations, effective February 1. Museum describes skills-based assessment and retained sponsorship distinctions.

name: New Part I regulations take effect
summary: Effective date specified in January 18 order.

name: Points-system regulations adopted
summary: Amends Part I regulations under P.C.1962-86, effective October 1; museum describes points-based selection of independent immigrants. Original ScheduleA pages now directly support its nine assessment factors; threshold/procedure pages not fully audited.

name: Points-system amendments take effect
summary: Effective date in the adopting order, distinct from August approval and September Gazette publication.

name: Immigration Act, 1976 assented in 1977
summary: Section 1 names the law Immigration Act, 1976, while the heading expressly records assent August 5, 1977; refugee definition appears in s.2.

name: 1978 commencement date: conflicting secondary accounts
summary: Museum reports April1,1978; McGill Law Journal footnote16 cites April10,1978 and SI/78-70. Event_date retains the museum-reported date only, NOT a verified legal commencement. Original proclamation must decide the conflict.

name: Singh: refugee determination fairness
summary: Appeals allowed, lower decisions set aside and claims remitted for merits hearings. Three judges relied on Charter s.7 and three on Canadian Bill of Rights s.2(e); not a universal right to admission.

name: Sections 1 and 4 in force.
summary: Sections 1 and 4 in force.

name: IRPA receives royal assent
summary: Immigration and Refugee Protection Act creates the successor framework for immigration and refugee protection; assent precedes phased commencement.

name: Sections 2,3,5–72,74–109,112–170,172–193,196–244 and 246–274 in force; not every section commenced then.
summary: Sections 2,3,5–72,74–109,112–170,172–193,196–244 and 246–274 in force; not every section commenced then.

name: Sections 73,110,111,171,194 and 195 in force; distinct later phase including appeal provisions.
summary: Sections 73,110,111,171,194 and 195 in force; distinct later phase including appeal provisions.

name: Strengthening Canada’s Immigration System and Borders Act
summary: Live Justice annual-statute page confirms title/citation and March 26 assent; IRPA consolidation identifies amendments by this chapter. Provision-specific commencement and full scope are queued.

name: IRPA live consolidation status
summary: Justice landing page says current to October 19, 2026 and last amended March 26, 2026; this is a website currency statement, not proof of no enactments after October 19.

name: IRPR live consolidation status
summary: Justice landing says current to October 19, 2026; last amended July 15, 2026; ten-row recent-amendments panel is not the complete amendment history.

name: Provincial allocation trigger under 1902 amendment
summary: The statute expressly makes the new one-half net entrance-tax allocation operate from July 1, 1902, subject to prescribed conditions; remittance is at fiscal-year end. This is not labeled commencement of the entire amendment.

name: An Act to amend the Immigration Act
summary: Inserts R.S.C.1886 c.65 s.24a authorizing disease-related landing prohibitions or conditional medical admission, including transit passengers; s.2 supplies apprehension, return and carrier penalties.

name: An Act to amend the Chinese Immigration Act, 1900
summary: Replaces 1900 c.32 s.24: revenues enter Consolidated Revenue Fund; one-half net entrance-tax proceeds allocated to collecting provinces from July 1, 1902, subject to orders and conditions.

name: An Act to amend The Chinese Immigration Act
summary: Adds a minister definition; revises exempt classes, student refunds and inland tax payments; replaces evasion offences and inserts s.27A apprehension/deportation provisions.

name: An Act to amend the Immigration Act
summary: Revises domicile, reporting, re-entry after removal, deportation direction, carrier return obligations and summary enforcement. Six amendment sections replace or modify 1910 Act ss.2(d),40,42(4),45,46,76.

name: Approval of cancellation of P.C.1911-1324
summary: LAC catalogue records approval October 5, 1911, following introduction and consideration October 4, of cancellation of the August 12 prohibition. The signed instrument, legal effective wording and enforcement history remain unread.

name: An Act to confer certain powers upon the Governor in Council and to amend the Immigration Act
summary: War Measures Act: s.12 adds Immigration Act s.3(2), restricting return/remain rights of residents leaving to serve a country at war with the Crown or aid its enemies, except ministerial permission. Section 2 retrospectively validates qualifying acts since August 1; that is not the assent date.

name: An Act to amend the Chinese Immigration Act
summary: Adds clergy and higher-education student exemptions, repeals the earlier student tax-refund subsection, and inserts ss.7a–7b governing loss of exemption, $500 tax, deportation and summary determination.

name: An Act respecting the Department of Immigration and Colonization
summary: Creates the statutory departmental/ministerial framework and transfers administration of the general and Chinese immigration Acts and related War Measures orders. Section 5 validates the minister’s exercise of powers since October 12, 1917; that reference is not this Act’s assent date.

name: An Act to amend an Act of the present session entitled An Act to amend The Immigration Act
summary: Repeals and replaces s.15 of the same-session c.25, itself replacing 1910 Act s.41, concerning deportation for specified political conduct or affiliations; the exception specifies British subjects born or naturalized in Canada. Both c.25 and c.26 received assent June 6, not separate dates weeks apart.

name: An Act to amend the Chinese Immigration Act
summary: Changes certificate evidence and ministerial finality, inquiry procedure, general-Act prohibited-class application, return-tax period from twelve months to two years, unregistered return taxation, warrantless examination/removal, offence procedure and imprisonment for unpaid fines.

name: An Act to amend The Immigration Act
summary: Initial sections add accredited international-trade-union representatives to the relevant definition, revise entry/station definitions and Boards of Inquiry. This summary covers ss.1–5 only; remaining provisions await a section-complete audit.

name: An Act to amend The Immigration Act
summary: Initial provisions repeal s.3(p), alter s.3(s), adjust investigation and re-entry provisions, and revise crew-list/security rules. This is an index-discovered amendment with a selective summary, not a complete provision inventory.

name: 1923 commencement mechanism remains unresolved
summary: Original c.38 gives June 30 assent and no explicit commencement clause. R.S.C.1906 Interpretation Act s.7(2) makes assent the default unless later commencement is provided. This creates a question, not proof overturning the official-history July 1 date: intervening Interpretation amendments and Gazette/implementation instruments require checking.

name: Interwar landing restrictions adopted
summary: Replaces earlier orders and prohibits landing except listed nationality/status, agricultural and dependent exceptions. The order excludes its permissions for persons described by its historical racial clause; this is attributed source classification, not a present-day label.

name: Date stated for operation of1931 restrictions
summary: Order approved March21 expressly says from and after March18,1931. This records its stated retrospective operation; actual enforcement on March18 has not been established.

name: First five-year immigration plan tabled
summary: McDougall tabled the five-year plan and proposed increases to220,000 in1991 and250,000 in1992 and beyond. These are planned admissions, not actual arrivals or a new Act.

name: First processing-priority instructions
summary: Original Gazette text now directly read. IRPA87.3 authority and87.3(6)publication notice; expressly effective on Gazette publication; applies to applications made on/afterFebruary27,2008.38 occupations or arranged employment or eligible in-Canada worker/student routes. No individual signature or separate making-date printed in this notice.

name: Instruction-based intake caps and eligibility revisions
summary: Original Gazette text now directly read. IRPA87.3 authority and87.3(6)publication notice; effective publication date; same-date application-receipt rule.20,000 non-arranged-employment applications,1,000 perNOC; first cap yearJune26,2010–June30,2011.29 occupations,language tests,CEC requirement and investor pause. No named signature/separate making-date printed.

name: Express Entry instructions signed
summary: Signed instructions establish electronic application management and ranking, with an express later commencement date.

name: Express Entry instructions take effect
summary: Section35 expressly fixes January1,2015 commencement. Launch, first invitation round and later admissions are separate events.

name: 2016 immigration levels plan
summary: Announced planned range280,000–305,000 new permanent residents, with emphasis on family reunification. Targets are not actual admissions.

name: 2021–2023 levels plan
summary: Announced permanent-resident targets401,000/411,000/421,000 for2021/2022/2023. Policy targets, not an amendment of IRPA or actual arrivals.

name: 2024–2026 levels plan
summary: Announced485,000 permanent residents for2024 and500,000 for2025 and2026. Later plans supersede these forward targets; not current2026 admissions law.

name: Reduced2025–2027 targets and temporary-resident planning
summary: Announced permanent-resident targets395,000/380,000/365,000 for2025/2026/2027, replacing the prior500,000 trajectory, and included temporary-resident targets for the first time. Government explanations/forecasts are attributed claims, not proven causal findings.

name: 2027–2029 levels targets released
summary: Live official page,issuedNovember5,2026,sets380,000 annual permanent-resident admissions and370,000 new temporary-resident arrivals for2027–2029; latter includes220,000 workers and150,000 students. Later-year targets are notional and subject to revision. These are a published plan, NOT future laws or actual outcomes.

name: Study-permit application cap announced
summary: Announced two-year intake cap expected to yield about360,000 approved study permits in2024, with stated exemptions and attestation requirements.360,000 is expected approvals, NOT the legal number of applications allowed; original instruction number remains open.

name: Low-wage Temporary Foreign Worker changes take effect
summary: September18 release specifies September26 effective changes, including lower workforce cap, processing restrictions and shorter employment duration subject to exceptions. Announcement is primary evidence of the stated implementation date; enabling instrument mapping remains open.

name: 1952 Immigration Act commencement proclamation: made and effectiveJune1,1953
summary: Original proclamation recitesS.C.1952c.42 and itsJuly4,1952 assent. MadeJune1,1953 and expressly brings the Act into force upon,from and afterJune1,1953; first published inCanadaGazetteJune20,1953. Publication is the primary official printing of the proclamation,with a distinct publication date. No unique proclamation number established.

summary: In five buyer suits over 69 Olympic Village units (REDMA rescission claims against the City and the building sales companies), the buyers had dropped their alternative misrepresentation claims. name: BC Supreme Court dismisses MSEFC property transfer tax petition (2010 BCSC 1156)
summary: MSEFC asked the court to declare that, when it bought the Olympic Village land from the City, property transfer tax would not apply to the value of the buildings it had paid to build. The court dismissed the petition as premature, saying the Property Transfer Tax Act's assessment and appeal process must be followed first, and added that on the merits the buildings would be part of the land's fair market value. Costs to the Crown.

summary: Opposition member Mr. Schmidt moved a spring 2026 meeting schedule that would include audit-focused meetings on the Auditor General's report 'An Examination of Community Laboratory Services (Contract with DynaLife)' and the Auditor General's upcoming report on Alberta Health Services procurement practices. The motion was defeated 3-6 (for: Ellingson, Eremenko, Schmidt; against: Lunty, van Dijken, Sawyer, Rowswell, Wiebe, Lovely); a second Schmidt motion for two audit-focused meetings was also defeated. In debate Mr. Schmidt quoted remarks he attributed to the Premier on AHS procurement. What stopped it: Recorded votes 3-6; Chair announced 'This motion is defeated.'

name: B.C. Bill 15 time-allocation motion: leave refused (May 28, 2025)
