name: Alberta's Bill 50 repealed municipal codes of conduct, ending Calgary's integrity commissioner complaint process (Edmonton affected too)
summary: Municipal Affairs Minister Ric McIver introduced Bill 50 on April 8, 2025 to eliminate mandatory municipal codes of conduct. The City of Calgary says its Code of Conduct Bylaw 26M2018 was repealed in May 2025 and its Integrity Commissioner no longer takes complaints. Stopped (as reported): Bill 50 introduced April 8, 2025; Calgary's bylaw repealed May 2025; complaints no longer accepted (by: Government of Alberta (Municipal Affairs Minister Ric McIver), Bill 50).

name: Crown stayed ASIRT's assault charge against Edmonton Const. Dylan Awid without giving a public reason
summary: ASIRT charged Edmonton Police Service Const. Dylan Awid with assault in October 2021 over force allegedly used after a handcuffed arrest on June 11, 2019. The Crown stayed the charge on Nov. 8, 2021, and neither the ministry nor ACPS gave a reason by deadline (Edmonton Journal). Stopped (as reported): Charge stayed Nov. 8, 2021. The ministry said only that ACPS's prosecution standard is higher than the police standard (by: Alberta Crown Prosecution Service (stay)).

name: ASIRT charges against Calgary police Const. Christopher Huggins over a 2022 shooting stayed by the Crown
summary: ASIRT charged a Calgary Police Service constable with aggravated assault and careless use of a firearm over a December 2022 arrest in which a man was shot. The charges were stayed on Feb. 9, 2026. Stopped (as reported): Charges stayed Feb. 9, 2026 (by: Alberta Crown Prosecution Service (stay)).

name: Alberta Crown declined ASIRT's recommendation to charge a second RCMP officer over a 2020 Maskwacis arrest
summary: ASIRT found several instances of assault by two RCMP officers during a Nov. 14, 2020 arrest in Maskwacis, which was largely captured on in-car video. Alberta Crown Prosecution Service said charges against Subject Officer #2 would not meet the reasonable-likelihood-of-conviction threshold; charges against Subject Officer #1 proceeded. Stopped (as reported): ACPS declined to prosecute the second officer; ASIRT accepted the opinion and laid no charge (by: Alberta Crown Prosecution Service).

name: Crown stayed ASIRT's assault-causing-bodily-harm charge against Edmonton Const. Michael Zacharuk after obtaining an outside use-of-force opinion
summary: Everett Rain suffered a skull fracture in the Edmonton police cellblock in November 2019. ASIRT charged Const. Michael Zacharuk with assault causing bodily harm (ASIRT release, Feb. 17, 2022). The Crown later stayed the charge after receiving an opinion from use-of-force expert Brad Fawcett. In February 2025, Chief Dale McFee found a reasonable prospect of a misconduct finding but held no disciplinary hearing. Stopped (as reported): Crown stayed proceedings after an out-of-province use-of-force opinion (exact stay date not given in the fetched sources). Chief McFee's decision of Feb. 6, 2025 cited the stay in declining a hearing (by: Alberta Crown Prosecution Service (stay)).

name: Crown declined charges against Vancouver officers after B.C.'s IIO forwarded a report on Myles Gray's 2015 death
summary: Myles Gray died after an encounter with Vancouver police in Burnaby in August 2015. The Independent Investigations Office sent a report to Crown counsel for consideration of charges in January 2019. The B.C. Prosecution Service announced no charges on Dec. 16, 2020. The OPCC then ordered a Police Act investigation (CBC). Stopped (as reported): BCPS clear statement: no charges approved (by: B.C. Prosecution Service (charge assessment)).

name: B.C.'s all-party Police Act reform recommendations (2022) were largely unimplemented three years later, with no timeline
summary: The Special Committee on Reforming the Police Act reported on April 28, 2022 with 11 recommendations, including a provincial police service and First Nations police governance. In April 2025 critics said progress had stalled. Solicitor General Garry Begg said all recommendations would be implemented but gave no timeline. Stopped (as reported): Only Bill 17 (Police Amendment Act, April 2024) passed, which critics called 'transactional'. No timeline for the rest (by: Government of British Columbia (implementation not completed)).

name: Citizen recall petition against Calgary Mayor Jyoti Gondek declared insufficient; recall did not proceed
summary: Under Alberta's 2022 recall provisions in the Municipal Government Act, Landon Johnston filed a notice to recall Mayor Jyoti Gondek on Jan. 30, 2024 and had Feb. 5 to April 4, 2024 to collect 514,284 signatures (40% of the 2019 population). On May 13, 2024 City Clerk Kate Martin declared the petition insufficient: 69,344 unverified petitioners, and zero valid signatures in a 369-signature random sample because the notice of recall was missing from the petition pages (MGA s. 240.7(3)(c)). Stopped (as reported): City Clerk declared the petition insufficient at a special council meeting on May 13, 2024 (by: Calgary City Clerk Kate Martin (statutory threshold under MGA Part 7.1 not met)).

name: Calgary's Green Line LRT wound down after Alberta withdrew its $1.53B commitment
summary: The Green Line, Calgary's largest-ever infrastructure project, had federal, provincial and city funding. On Sept. 3, 2024 Transportation Minister Devin Dreeshen wrote that the province would withdraw its $1.53 billion; on Sept. 17, 2024 council voted 10-5 to wind the project down. Stopped (as reported): Province withdrew funding (Dreeshen letter, Sept. 3, 2024); council voted 10-5 on Sept. 17, 2024 to wind down; Coun. Sonya Sharp's amendment to pause instead was defeated (by: Government of Alberta (Transportation Minister Devin Dreeshen) withdrawing funding; Calgary council 10-5 wind-down vote).

name: Release of the CRCC's Colten Boushie report was held up nearly 11 months awaiting the RCMP Commissioner's response
summary: The CRCC sent its interim report on the RCMP's investigation of Colten Boushie's 2016 death to Commissioner Brenda Lucki on Jan. 21, 2020. The final report cannot be released until the Commissioner responds, and that response did not come until Dec. 4, 2020, beyond the six-month target reported by CBC and the Globe. The final report was released Jan. 7, 2021. Stopped (as reported): Commissioner's response arrived Dec. 4, 2020; final report Jan. 7, 2021. The Globe reported RCMP backlogs prevented release (by: RCMP Commissioner's delayed response (Brenda Lucki)).

name: Edmonton council shelved, in a closed session, its auditor's proposed audit of the police commission and police service
summary: City Auditor Hoa Quach proposed a scope for reviewing the Edmonton Police Commission and the Edmonton Police Service's $384.8M 2022 budget. After going in camera for legal advice on Monday, Jan. 24, 2022, council did not vote on the audit, and no reason was given in public (Edmonton Journal). Stopped (as reported): After an in-camera session, council took no vote and gave no direction. The mayor's office said any revised audit would need the commission's consent to share records (by: Edmonton City Council (closed session)).

name: Edmonton Police Commission refused council's request for an EPS internal-audit plan and said a program-services review would not be done
summary: In December 2023, council asked the commission for an audit plan showing which parts of the Edmonton Police Service were being audited, and for a program-services review. In an April 19, 2024 letter, the commission refused to share internal audit plan information and said no program-services review would be undertaken (Global News). Stopped (as reported): Commission letter of April 19, 2024 declining both. Chair John McDougall said the commission 'already regularly audits the police service' (by: Edmonton Police Commission).

name: Manitoba's IIU 2016-17 annual report was never tabled until a Free Press series exposed it
summary: The Independent Investigation Unit's 2016-17 annual report was delivered to Manitoba Justice but not made public. After a Winnipeg Free Press series found it missing, Justice Minister Cliff Cullen tabled it on Nov. 21, 2018, calling the omission 'an administrative error'. Stopped (as reported): Not tabled until Nov. 21, 2018; Cullen said the report was never received by his predecessor (by: Manitoba Justice (Minister Cliff Cullen)).

name: Manitoba never launched a search for a permanent IIU civilian director after Roxanne Gagné resigned in October 2024
summary: Freedom-of-information records obtained by the Investigative Journalism Foundation show 'no competition' and 'no records' of a hiring process for a permanent director of the Independent Investigation Unit between Jan. 1, 2024 and July 7, 2026. Bruce Sychuk has been acting director since November 2024. Stopped (as reported): No competition held as of July 7, 2026 (FOI response). The acting designation stays in force until a civilian director revokes it (by: Government of Manitoba (no competition launched)).

name: Montreal council blocked an opposition motion for an independent inquiry into discriminatory-harassment complaint handling in the city public service
summary: Opposition leader Aref Salem sought to add item 65.03, a motion for an independent inquiry into how discriminatory-harassment complaints are handled and into the work climate in Montreal's public service. Under by-law 06-051 art. 32, adding the item needed unanimous consent, which was refused. A recorded vote failed 23-37. Stopped (as reported): Coun. François Limoges invoked art. 32 (unanimous consent). Majority leader Alex Norris said the administration did not support adding the item. The previous question was moved, and the recorded vote failed 23-37 (by: Montreal council majority (Projet Montréal) refusing unanimous consent; recorded vote 23-37).

name: Quebec named an observer instead of ordering an independent investigation of alleged racism by Montréal-Nord SPVM officers
summary: Two Station 39 officers were suspended and 16 investigated over alleged racist and hateful acts. Community groups called for an independent investigation. Minister Ian Lafrenière left the SPVM in charge of its own investigation and appointed lawyer Anne-Marie Boisvert as an independent observer, saying a public inquiry was not ruled out after the criminal investigation. Stopped (as reported): Minister appointed observer Anne-Marie Boisvert (June 20, 2026). The SPVM keeps both the criminal and the disciplinary probes (by: Quebec Minister of Domestic Security Ian Lafrenière (observer appointed instead; BEI not assigned)).

name: Montreal decided not to equip SPVM officers with body cameras after a year-long pilot
summary: The SPVM ran a body-camera pilot with 78 officers and reported on Jan. 29, 2019 that full rollout would cost $17.4M over five years plus $24M a year. Mayor Valérie Plante announced on Feb. 6, 2019 that the city would not go ahead. Stopped (as reported): Plante announced at the executive committee that the city would not proceed, citing cost. Axon said the estimate was inflated (by: City of Montreal administration (Mayor Valérie Plante)).

name: Montreal council rejected an opposition motion asking the auditor general to probe Quebec gun-violence funds for the SPVM
summary: After the Journal de Montréal reported that Quebec questioned how Montreal used provincial money meant for the SPVM, Ensemble Montréal asked council to have the vérificatrice générale investigate. Council rejected the motion on Tuesday, Sept. 20, 2022 (Journal Métro). Stopped (as reported): Motion rejected by the Projet Montréal majority. Executive committee chair Dominique Ollivier called the insinuations 'graves, inacceptables et fausses' (by: Montreal council majority (Projet Montréal)).

name: Promised independent probe of police conduct in Glen Assoun's wrongful conviction stalled for years after B.C.'s IIO withdrew
summary: In September 2020, Nova Scotia's justice minister asked SIRT to investigate possible police criminal misconduct before Glen Assoun's appeal. SIRT engaged B.C.'s IIO in March 2021. On April 18, 2023 the IIO withdrew, citing workload. By May 2025 no agency had taken over. An agreement with an Alberta team was later reported. Stopped (as reported): IIOBC withdrew on April 18, 2023 (workload and resources). The case was 'in limbo' as of May 2025 (by: IIO B.C. withdrawal; no replacement investigator until 2025).

name: Ontario paused the Safer Ontario Act's oversight overhaul in 2018; the replacement law took effect only in April 2024
summary: The Liberal government passed the Safer Ontario Act in 2018, overhauling police oversight including the SIU and police boards. After winning power, Doug Ford's government paused its implementation, calling it anti-police. Its replacement, the Community Safety and Policing Act (2019), took effect on April 1, 2024, five years after passage. Stopped (as reported): Paused by the new government (2018). The CSPA, passed 2019, was in force April 1, 2024; the government cited bill size, regulations and COVID-19 (by: Government of Ontario (Premier Doug Ford) pausing the Safer Ontario Act). Canada Records Collector record (on-safer-ontario-act-police-oversight-never-proclaimed-2019): Ontario's Safer Ontario Act, 2018 (new Inspector General of Policing, Policing Oversight Act, expanded SIU) passed but its main schedules were never proclaimed; repealed in 2019 and replaced, with the new regime only in force in April 2024.

name: Ottawa police board's hiring of Matt Torigian as interim chief undone after council ousted board chair Diane Deans
summary: During the 2022 convoy occupation, after Chief Peter Sloly resigned, the Ottawa Police Services Board under chair Diane Deans engaged former Waterloo chief Matt Torigian as interim chief. Council voted 15-9 on Feb. 16, 2022 to remove Deans as chair; Torigian withdrew Feb. 17 and Steve Bell remained interim chief. Stopped (as reported): Council voted 15-9 to remove Deans as chair (motion by Scott Moffatt and Laura Dudas, per Ottawa Citizen); Eli El-Chantiry became chair; Torigian withdrew Feb. 17, 2022 (by: Ottawa City Council (15-9 vote removing board chair); Matt Torigian withdrawal).

name: Ottawa council rejected a judicial inquiry into the Confederation Line LRT, 13-10
summary: Coun. Catherine McKenney twice sought a judicial inquiry into the procurement and launch of Ottawa's Confederation Line. An October 2021 attempt was blocked procedurally and replaced by an auditor-general probe; on Nov. 10, 2021 council voted 13-10 against an inquiry. (Ontario later called a public inquiry; not sourced here.) Stopped (as reported): Defeated 13-10; Mayor Watson and 12 councillors voted against, preferring the auditor general's non-public audit (by: Ottawa City Council majority (13-10), incl. Mayor Jim Watson).

name: Quebec's BEI is the only police oversight body in Canada whose final investigation reports are never made public
summary: Ten years after it began (2016) and with about 490 investigations opened, the Bureau des enquêtes indépendantes still does not publish its final reports (CBC). Director Brigitte Bishop said the BEI's constituting act does not allow more transparency and that legislative changes are being worked on with the ministry. Stopped (as reported): BEI says its act does not permit publication. The minister's office did not respond to CBC (by: Quebec Police Act framework; Quebec government (no legislative change yet)).

name: SIU aggravated-assault charge against Toronto Det. Const. Christian Campoli withdrawn by the Crown before trial
summary: Ontario's Special Investigations Unit charged a Toronto police detective constable with aggravated assault after a bystander was seriously injured during a downtown arrest in August 2024. The Crown withdrew the charge in January 2026 after a preliminary inquiry. Stopped (as reported): Charge withdrawn by the Crown; the Toronto Police Association said the preliminary-inquiry judge found 'no reasonable prospect of conviction' (by: Crown (Ontario) after preliminary inquiry).

name: Ontario Bill 5 cut Toronto council from 47 to 25 wards mid-campaign, overriding the city's planned 2018 ward structure
summary: Toronto's 2018 municipal election was under way on a 47-ward map when the province passed the Better Local Government Act, 2018 (Bill 5), cutting council to 25 wards. A Superior Court judge struck the law down on Sept. 10, 2018; the Court of Appeal stayed that ruling and the election went ahead on 25 wards; the Supreme Court of Canada later upheld the law 5-4. Stopped (as reported): Bill 5 received royal assent Aug. 14, 2018 and imposed 25 wards. Belobaba J. struck it down Sept. 10, 2018; the Court of Appeal for Ontario stayed that order Sept. 19, 2018 (2018 ONCA 761), so the vote proceeded on 25 wards; the SCC upheld the Act Oct. 1, 2021 (2021 SCC 34) (by: Government of Ontario (Premier Doug Ford) via Bill 5; Court of Appeal for Ontario stay; Supreme Court of Canada).

name: Integrity commissioner probe of ex-councillor Justin Di Ciano was suspended for a police referral, then terminated after OPP charges were withdrawn
summary: A 2016 code-of-conduct complaint about then-councillor Justin Di Ciano was suspended in 2017 when the integrity commissioner referred matters to police. OPP charges under the Municipal Elections Act laid in 2018 were withdrawn in 2020, and the integrity commissioner then terminated the inquiry. Stopped (as reported): Suspended Aug. 11, 2017 on referral to police; OPP charged Di Ciano Nov. 16, 2018; charges withdrawn Feb. 24, 2020; inquiry terminated in a December 2020 report to council (by: Integrity Commissioners Valerie Jepson (suspension, 2017) and Jonathan Batty (termination, 2020); Crown withdrawal of OPP charges).

name: Toronto integrity commissioner suspended a complaint probe into Mayor John Tory's Rogers-related vote because of the 2022 election freeze
summary: A complaint alleged Mayor John Tory should not have voted on an ActiveTO road-closure item affecting the Rogers-owned Blue Jays. Integrity Commissioner Jonathan Batty said he could not finish before the election-period cut-off and suspended the inquiry. Stopped (as reported): Batty said he could not complete the inquiry before the Aug. 19, 2022 cut-off after which no code-of-conduct report can go to council during the election period; file suspended (by: Integrity Commissioner Jonathan Batty, applying the election-period reporting freeze).

name: Coroner's inquest into Regis Korchinski-Paquet's 2020 death adjourned indefinitely just before closing submissions
summary: The inquest into the May 27, 2020 death of Regis Korchinski-Paquet, who fell from a 24th-floor balcony while Toronto police were in her home, finished hearing evidence and was due for closing submissions when the presiding coroner adjourned it 'until further notice' for an 'unanticipated investigation'. The SIU had earlier cleared police; that finding was disputed (CBC/CP). Stopped (as reported): Coroner Dr. David Cameron adjourned the inquest indefinitely, citing 'quite unanticipated investigation that needs to be done', with no details (by: Presiding coroner Dr. David Cameron).

name: Staff plan to end 10 of Vancouver's 11 council advisory committees early was pulled from the agenda before the vote
summary: City staff recommended ending the terms of 10 of 11 volunteer council advisory committees on Jan. 30, 2026 instead of Nov. 1, 2026, citing staff capacity during the World Cup and election year. The report was withdrawn less than a day before the council meeting, with no explanation given. Stopped (as reported): Report quietly withdrawn from the agenda; city said staff are 'considering alternative approaches' (by: City of Vancouver staff (report withdrawn from agenda)).

name: Vancouver council's freeze of the 2021 police budget was overturned by B.C.'s Director of Police Services
summary: In December 2020 Vancouver council declined to increase the Vancouver Police Department's 2021 budget. The Vancouver Police Board appealed under s. 27(3) of the Police Act; in March 2022 the provincial Director of Police Services ordered about $5.7 million restored. Mayor Kennedy Stewart called it 'the extraordinary removal of local democracy from the oversight of police' (CityNews). Stopped (as reported): Director of Police Services sided with the board (March 2022) and ordered funding restored; on April 12, 2022 council paid from reserves; Coun. Jean Swanson's motion to reject the decision did not pass (by: B.C. Director of Police Services on appeal by the Vancouver Police Board).

name: B.C. shelved the bill enabling dissolution of Vancouver's elected park board; the mayor later dropped the plan
summary: Mayor Ken Sim announced in December 2023 he wanted to abolish the elected Vancouver Board of Parks and Recreation. The province tabled enabling legislation Oct. 9, 2025, then said it would not call it for second reading after the Musqueam, Squamish and Tsleil-Waututh Nations asked for a pause. Sim dropped the plan in July 2026 (CTV). Stopped (as reported): Minister Christine Boyle told Sim the bill would not be called for second reading after an MST Nations letter asked it be 'immediately paused'; Sim later abandoned dissolution (by: B.C. Municipal Affairs Minister Christine Boyle (not calling bill for second reading) after MST Nations request; Mayor Ken Sim later dropped plan).

name: Manitoba refused to support a Prairie Green landfill search for the remains of Morgan Harris and Marcedes Myran
summary: An Indigenous-led feasibility committee found a search of the Prairie Green landfill feasible, at up to three years and $184M with no guarantee of finding remains. On July 5, 2023 Premier Heather Stefanson told Indigenous leaders and those calling for the search that the province would support a memorial but not a search, citing worker safety. Winnipeg police had earlier declined to search (CityNews, Dec. 2022). Stopped (as reported): Province declined to fund or support a search (July 5, 2023) (by: Government of Manitoba (Premier Heather Stefanson)).

name: After the RCMP's Winnipeg police HQ probe ended without charges, Manitoba refused the city's request for a public inquiry for more than five years
summary: In February 2017, council asked the province for a public inquiry into the police headquarters project and other real-estate and procurement matters. Premier Brian Pallister said there would be none while the RCMP investigated (Project Dalton). On Dec. 13, 2019 the Manitoba Prosecution Service authorized no charges, and Justice Minister Cliff Cullen said there would be no inquiry. In July 2023 the Stefanson government held that position, citing litigation. The province later called a focused police-HQ inquiry (CBC, 2025). Stopped (as reported): MPS: no charges ('not a reasonable likelihood of conviction'). Cullen: no inquiry (Dec. 13, 2019). Premier Heather Stefanson reaffirmed the refusal in July 2023 (by: Manitoba Prosecution Service (no charges); Pallister and Stefanson governments (inquiry refused)).

name: Cyber security C-26 ended prorogation (2025)
summary: Government Bill C-26, An Act respecting cyber security, amending the Telecommunications Act and making consequential amendments to other Acts, sponsored by the Minister of Public Safety, Democratic Institutions and Intergovernmental Affairs, was introduced in the 44th Parliament, 1st session. LEGISinfo records its final status for that session (November 22, 2021 to January 6, 2025) as 'At consideration in the House of Commons of amendments made by the Senate' (latest activity: Message sent to the House of Commons on Thursday, December 5, 2024 (Senate); House third reading completed June 19, 2024); it did not reach Royal Assent. The session ended with the Proclamation Proroguing Parliament to March 24, 2025 (SI/2025-9, January 6, 2025). What stopped it: Prorogation of Parliament on January 6, 2025 ended the session with the bill still unfinished.

name: Digital charter C-27 ended prorogation (2025)
summary: Government Bill C-27, An Act to enact the Consumer Privacy Protection Act, the Personal Information and Data Protection Tribunal Act and the Artificial Intelligence and Data Act ... (Digital Charter Implementation Act, 2022), sponsored by the Minister of Innovation, Science and Industry, was introduced in the 44th Parliament, 1st session. LEGISinfo records its final status for that session (November 22, 2021 to January 6, 2025) as 'At consideration in committee in the House of Commons' (latest activity: Second reading and referral to committee on Monday, April 24, 2023); it did not reach Royal Assent. The session ended with the Proclamation Proroguing Parliament to March 24, 2025 (SI/2025-9, January 6, 2025). What stopped it: Prorogation of Parliament on January 6, 2025 ended the session with the bill still unfinished.

name: ETHI SNC-Lavalin study refused (2019-03-26)
summary: Peter Kent moved that ETHI immediately begin a study of what the motion called the ongoing corruption scandal involving the Prime Minister, that the Chair write to the Prime Minister requesting he waive constraints, that Jody Wilson-Raybould and Jane Philpott be invited by April 5, and that the Committee report to Parliament. A Tracey Ramsey amendment was negatived 3-6 and the motion was negatived 3-6. What stopped it: Motion negatived on recorded division 3-6 (YEAS: Gourde, Kent, Ramsey; NAYS: Erskine-Smith, Fortier, de Burgh Graham, Lauzon, Picard, Saini).

name: ETHI-summoned ministerial staff did not appear (2021)
summary: On March 25, 2021 the House adopted (Division No. 80, 181-153) Michael Barrett's motion, as amended, ordering Rick Theis, Amitpal Singh and Ben Chin to appear before ETHI (and Zita Astravas before NDDN) on WE Charity / Canada Student Service Grant matters, with the Prime Minister able to appear instead for three hours. ETHI minutes record the witnesses' absence, that the committee had not released them, and that Ministers Pablo Rodriguez and Mona Fortier appeared after ordering the staff not to appear. What stopped it: The staff did not appear; ministers appeared in their place after instructing them not to attend. The committee recorded their non-attendance.

name: ETHI trudeau II report witnesses refused (2019-08-21)
summary: After the Conflict of Interest and Ethics Commissioner's Trudeau II Report, ETHI met in August 2019. Peter Kent's motion to invite the Commissioner to brief the Committee on his report was negatived 4-5; Charlie Angus's motion to invite Prime Minister Justin Trudeau, Finance Minister Bill Morneau, adviser Ben Chin and the Clerk of the Privy Council (to explain not sharing Cabinet confidences with the Commissioner, who felt his investigation was hampered) was negatived 3-6; and Lisa Raitt's motion requesting author Aaron Wherry's interview materials was negatived 2-7. What stopped it: Three motions negatived on recorded divisions: Kent 4-5 (NAYS Baylis, Fortier, MacKinnon, McCrimmon, Vandenbeld); Angus 3-6; Raitt 2-7. Committee adjourned to the call of the Chair.

name: FINA WE documents redacted (2020)
summary: Pierre Poilievre's motion before FINA proposed reporting to the House that the Committee's July 7, 2020 order for WE Charity / Me to We contract and CSSG documents (redactions to be made by the Law Clerk) had not been complied with, quoting the Law Clerk that departments had redacted on grounds not contemplated in the order and that his Office had not seen the unredacted documents; it also noted that the August 18, 2020 prorogation prevented consideration. An amendment and a Gerretsen subamendment (suspending debate until testimony on the redactions) were debated across meetings from October 15 to November 19, 2020, with the meeting of October 28 running, with suspensions, to November 4, and meeting 5 running to November 19, when an 11-0 compromise set a November 24 deadline for unredacted documents (except ATIA s.69) to the Law Clerk and appearances by the Clerk of the Privy Council and the Ethics Commissioner. What stopped it: Departments redacted on grounds the Law Clerk said were not contemplated by the order; the motion to report non-compliance to the House was then held up for weeks of debate and suspensions (meetings 2, 4 and 5) before being replaced by a negotiated compromise.

name: House anti corruption committee defeated (2020-10-21)
summary: Erin O'Toole moved, seconded by Gérard Deltell, that a special committee (the 'Anti-Corruption Committee') be appointed to examine matters including the Canada Student Service Grant, WE Charity's relationships with the government, the Canada Emergency Commercial Rent Assistance program and lobbying-related allegations. An amendment was negatived (Division No. 10, 143-181) and the main motion was negatived (Division No. 11, 146-180). What stopped it: Amendment negatived (Division No. 10, YEAS 143, NAYS 181); main motion negatived (Division No. 11, YEAS 146, NAYS 180).

name: House motion for a Huawei 5G decision within 30 days not met (2020)
summary: The House agreed (Division No. 23, 178-146) to Michael Chong's motion, seconded by Pierre Paul-Hus, calling on the government to decide on Huawei's involvement in Canada's 5G network within 30 days and to table, within 30 days, a plan to combat China's foreign operations and intimidation. ISED's policy statement announcing the intent to prohibit Huawei and ZTE in 5G networks is dated May 19, 2022. What stopped it: The Huawei decision was announced on May 19, 2022 (about 18 months later). This record set does not establish whether or when the plan in part (b) was tabled.

name: House SNC-Lavalin inquiry motion defeated (2019-02-20)
summary: Charlie Angus's opposition motion, seconded by Pierre-Luc Dusseault, called on the Prime Minister to waive solicitor-client privilege for the former Attorney General regarding the SNC-Lavalin prosecution matter and urged a public inquiry under the Inquiries Act. An amendment setting a May 31, 2019 reporting date was negatived (Division 991, 133-159) and the main motion was negatived (Division 992, 134-160). What stopped it: Amendment negatived (Division No. 991, YEAS 133, NAYS 159); main motion negatived (Division No. 992, YEAS 134, NAYS 160).

name: JUST SNC-Lavalin privilege waiver refused (2019-02-27)
summary: Murray Rankin moved that the Committee call upon the Prime Minister and Governor-in-Council to waive solicitor-client privilege and Cabinet confidentiality relating to the SNC-Lavalin issue so the former Attorney General could inform the Committee about the period after she ceased to serve as Attorney General on January 14, 2019. Debate was adjourned until questioning of the witness was completed; the motion was then negatived 4-5. What stopped it: Motion negatived on recorded division 4-5 (YEAS: Barrett, Cooper, Paul-Hus, Rankin; NAYS: Boissonnault, Ehsassi, Khalid, O'Connell, Sahota).

name: JUST SNC-Lavalin witnesses refused (2019-02-13)
summary: At JUST meeting 129 the Committee agreed (5-4) to hold meetings on remediation agreements, the Shawcross Doctrine and discussions between the Office of the Attorney General and Government colleagues, with witnesses David Lametti, Nathalie Drouin and Michael Wernick. An amendment by Nathan Cullen to add Jody Wilson-Raybould, Gerald Butts and Mathieu Bouchard as witnesses and delete 'in camera' was negatived 4-5; an amendment by Michael Cooper calling on the Prime Minister to waive privilege was ruled out of order by the Chair as beyond the scope of the motion; and a separate Cooper motion asking the Prime Minister to immediately waive solicitor-client privilege involving the former Attorney General in respect of the SNC-Lavalin matter was negatived 4-5. What stopped it: Cullen amendment negatived on recorded division 4-5 (YEAS: Barrett, Cooper, Cullen, Raitt; NAYS: Boissonnault, Ehsassi, Fraser, Khalid, McKinnon); Cooper amendment ruled out of order; Cooper waiver motion negatived 4-5.

name: Zita Astravas did not appear before NDDN as ordered by the House (2021)
summary: The House order of March 25, 2021 required Zita Astravas to appear before the National Defence committee on April 6, 2021. At NDDN meeting 23 that day, Minister of National Defence Harjit Sajjan appeared instead; James Bezan said this 'doesn't absolve Zita Astravas from appearing at committee'. NDDN meeting 31 minutes record a Bezan motion reciting that she was invited (Mar 8) and ordered by the House (Apr 6) and 'did not appear on either occasion'; an amendment deleting paragraph (b) carried 7-4 and the minutes show no final vote before adjournment. What stopped it: She did not appear; the Minister appeared instead. A later motion to pursue her appearance was amended and not brought to a final vote in the recorded meeting.

name: Ontario greenbelt committee study refused (2023-09-13)
summary: Mary-Margaret McMahon moved under Standing Order 113(a) that the Committee study the government's decision to remove lands from the Greenbelt, with public hearings September 27-October 3 and report writing October 5, inviting the former Minister of Municipal Affairs and Housing, associate and deputy ministers, the Provincial Land and Development Facilitator and potentially staff of the Premier's office and Cabinet Office. The motion was lost on a recorded vote (Ayes: Andrew, McMahon, Stevens; Nays: Babikian, Grewal, McGregor, Pang, Sabawy, Thanigasalam). What stopped it: Recorded vote: 3 ayes, 6 nays; Chair declared the motion lost.

name: Ontario PAC greenbelt witnesses refused (2024-03-25)
summary: France Gélinas moved that the Committee authorize inviting additional witnesses for its review of the Auditor General's Special Report on Changes to the Greenbelt, including a Ministry of Natural Resources and Forestry representative involved with repeal of the Duffins Rouge Agricultural Preserve Act, three named individuals, and ministry witnesses for the 2023 government advertising review. The motion was lost (Ayes: Gélinas; Nays: Bouma, Crawford, Sandhu, Skelly, Laura Smith). At the May 6, 2024 hearing MPP Jeff Burch called it unfortunate that government members did not extend an invitation to MNRF officials. What stopped it: Recorded vote 1-5; Chair declared the motion lost. Later hearing records that MNRF officials were not invited.

name: PACP never voted on John Nater motion for ArriveCAN subcontractor lists (Feb 15, 2024)
summary: At PACP meeting 100, John Nater moved a production motion. It would have ordered CBSA, PHAC, PSPC and other departments, the main ArriveCAN contractors (GC Strategies, Dalian Enterprises Incorporated, Amazon Web Services, Microsoft Canada, TEKsystems, Donna Cona, BDO Canada LLP, MGIS, 49 Solutions, Makwa Resourcing/TPG Technology Consulting, Advanced Chippewa Technologies) and the Auditor General to provide complete lists of ArriveCAN subcontractors or "Other" contractors, the services provided and the amounts paid, within seven days. It also ordered GC Strategies and departments to list all GC Strategies subcontractors since 2015. The minutes record "Debate arose thereon." and then "At 5:18 p.m., the committee adjourned to the call of the Chair." No vote is recorded. The evidence shows the bells were ringing; the Chair asked for unanimous consent to continue and members said no, and the meeting was adjourned. The motion does not appear in the minutes of PACP meetings 101 to 108 (Feb 20 to Mar 19, 2024). What stopped it: "Debate arose thereon." followed by "At 5:18 p.m., the committee adjourned to the call of the Chair." The evidence at block (1715) records the Chair: "The bells are ringing. Is there UC to continue to the bottom of the hour?"; "Some hon. members: No."; then "The meeting is adjourned." No recorded vote on the motion.

name: PESRA Part II never brought into force
summary: Part II of the Parliamentary Employment and Staff Relations Act (R.S.C. 1985, c. 33 (2nd Supp.)), 'Standard Hours, Wages, Leave, Etc.', is shown as not in force on the Justice Laws site and is listed as not in force on Dec 31, 2024 and Dec 31, 2025 in the Statutes Repeal Act annual reports (tabled May 28, 2025 and Feb 2-3, 2026). What stopped it: Never brought into force; still listed under the Statutes Repeal Act as not in force.

name: Ports c33 died prorogation (2025)
summary: The government's port-reform bill from the Ports Modernization Review (amending the Canada Marine Act, Marine Transportation Security Act and Customs Act) stalled at House report stage after one day of debate on Sept 20, 2024. It died when Parliament was prorogued on Jan 6, 2025, never reaching third reading or the Senate. What stopped it: LEGISinfo: 'Report stage Not completed'; 'Third reading Not reached'; Senate stages 'Not reached'; session Nov 22, 2021 to Jan 6, 2025. The Proclamation prorogued Parliament to March 24, 2025.

name: Ports mtscp held in reserve and narrowed
summary: Background checks for port workers were announced in January 2003 and recommended for all workers at major ports (SCONSAD 2002 Rec. 6). Transport Canada left the program out of the July 1, 2004 Marine Transportation Security Regulations ('held in reserve') and later narrowed it to designated duties and restricted areas. In April 2026 SECU testimony, a witness said under 20% of port workers hold clearances. What stopped it: 'Originally the MTSCP was to be included in the Regulations that came into force on July 1, 2004 ... However, to allow for more thorough consultations and policy development, it was held in reserve.' The program was then refocused on 'specific designated duties and smaller restricted areas'.

name: Ports pacp random exam fee recommendation rejected (2009)
summary: After the Auditor General's 2007 CBSA audit, PACP recommended that carriers chosen for random inspections not pay examination fees. The government accepted this 'only in part' and kept the fee process. In 2022 CBSA's own audit found 'the prohibitive cost of examinations' still shaped marine targeting. What stopped it: 'The Government accepts the fourth Committee recommendation only in part. ... it has concluded that the process of levying examination fees will not be changed.'

name: Ports ports canada police disbanded (1997)
summary: Canada's national port police (324 officers at its 1972 peak, per the Senate) was eliminated in 1997 and policing was devolved to local forces. In the House, Transport Minister Collenette defended the move as devolution and promised that 'crime will not increase'. What stopped it: The force was disbanded in 1997. In Question Period, Elsie Wayne asked why the minister was 'disbanding the Ports Canada police'. Collenette replied that it was devolution and 'We put this regime in place.'

name: Ports public inquiry recommended never called
summary: The Kenny committee recommended in 2002 and again in 2003 (Rec. 4.2) a public inquiry under the Inquiries Act into crime and terrorism vulnerabilities at Canada's ports. Transport Canada's July 7, 2006 response did not address it, and no such federal inquiry was held. What stopped it: The government response quoted in Seaports (Transport Canada, July 7, 2006) lists ISPS/MTSR, waterside security and MTSCP measures but, per the Committee, 'makes absolutely no reference to the recommendation, which calls for a public inquiry under the Inquiries Act'.

name: Ports rcmp port policing not restored
summary: In 2003 the Senate recommended re-creating the RCMP Marine Division, at least the former Ports Canada Police's size, to police major ports. By 2007 Transport Canada was still 'reviewing the issue of port policing'. The RCMP said about 900 personnel were needed, and the Committee found the RCMP 'has not even been adequately funded' to staff Halifax, Montreal and Vancouver. What stopped it: Seaports 2007: TC response says port policing is 'currently reviewing'; the Committee says 'The RCMP has not even been adequately funded to put meaningful contingents of officers at the ports of Halifax, Montreal, and Vancouver'. RCMP Asst. Commr. Souccar estimated '900 resources' were needed.

name: Quebec SAAQclic privilege motions rejected (2025-04)
summary: On April 8, 2025 the Official Opposition House Leader, Monsef Derraji, moved under Standing Orders 324 and 327 that the Commission de l'Assemblée nationale be mandated to examine whether the SAAQ and certain current and former executives intentionally gave erroneous information to the Commission de l'administration publique about the CASA/SAAQclic project; the referral motion was rejected 34-76. On April 9, 2025 a deferred vote on his motion that the Assembly declare that the SAAQ and certain executives breached the rights and privileges of the Assembly by intentionally transmitting erroneous information was rejected 31-75. What stopped it: Referral motion rejected (Pour 34, Contre 76); privilege motion rejected (Pour 31, Contre 75).

name: Arm's-length Alberta Environmental Monitoring, Evaluation and Reporting Agency (AEMERA) dissolved and folded into Alberta Environment and Parks (Bill 18, June 2016)
summary: AEMERA was created under the Protecting Alberta's Environment Act as an arm's-length agency to monitor and report on environmental conditions, notably in the oil sands. After Paul Boothe's review called it a 'failed experiment', Environment Minister Shannon Phillips announced on April 5, 2016 that monitoring would move into the department, overseen by a chief scientist (CBC). AEMERA's 2015-16 annual report says Bill 18 received royal assent May 27, 2016, repealing the Protecting Alberta's Environment Act, and AEMERA was dissolved effective June 30, 2016. Its functions went to a new Environmental Monitoring and Science Division. Stopped (as reported): Bill 18 repealed the Protecting Alberta's Environment Act; AEMERA dissolved effective June 30, 2016 (by: Government of Alberta (NDP), Minister of Environment and Parks Shannon Phillips; Legislature (Bill 18)).

name: Alberta Energy Regulator board chair and directors rescinded and replaced by an interim board chaired by a deputy minister (O.C. 156/2019, Sept 2019)
summary: O.C. 156/2019 (Sept 6, 2019), recommended by the Energy and Environment ministers under s.5 of the Responsible Energy Development Act, rescinded Sheila O'Brien's appointment as chair and the appointments of directors Brian Fleck, Monica Norminton and Jack Royal. It appointed an interim board to June 5, 2020: chair Beverly Yee (deputy minister of Environment and Parks, unpaid) with Sherri Brillon, David Goldie, Georgette Habib and Grant Sprague (King's Printer). Energy Minister Sonya Savage and Environment Minister Jason Nixon also launched a review of the AER's mandate. Media reported the board replacement and review followed a UCP campaign commitment (CBC, Global, Calgary Herald). Stopped (as reported): Cabinet order rescinded the chair's and three directors' appointments and installed an interim board (by: Lieutenant Governor in Council on recommendation of the Ministers of Energy and of Environment and Parks).

name: Alberta Health Minister Fred Horne fires the entire AHS board after it declined to cancel executive pay-at-risk bonuses; Janet Davidson named official administrator (June 2013)
summary: On June 12, 2013 Health Minister Fred Horne dismissed the whole Alberta Health Services board, including chair Stephen Lockwood. The day before, the board had declined a government directive to reconsider 2012-13 executive pay-at-risk payments. Janet Davidson was appointed official administrator to act in place of the board and review the bonus decision (CBC, Globe). Lockwood called it political interference (CBC). The board structure was restored in 2015 (Edmonton Journal, 2022). Stopped (as reported): Entire board dismissed without severance; official administrator appointed (by: Minister of Health Fred Horne (PC government)).

name: Alberta Health Services board (11 members) dismissed and replaced by a single official administrator, John Cowell (Ministerial Order 319/2022, Nov 2022)
summary: Ministerial Order 319/2022 (Health), dated Nov 17, 2022, 'dismisses all current members of the Alberta Health Services Board and appoints an official administrator in place of the board' (Open Government). Premier Danielle Smith and Health Minister Jason Copping named Dr. John Cowell, who reported to the minister (CBC). Copping said the board would be restored 'at the appropriate time' (Edmonton Journal). AHS's 2022-23 annual report says that under s.11 of the Regional Health Authorities Act the administrator holds the board's governance functions and is accountable to the Minister and Premier. The order was reappointed by MOs 305/2023 and 307/2023. Stopped (as reported): MO 319/2022 dismissed all board members and appointed an official administrator (by: Minister of Health Jason Copping (ministerial order), on the Premier's leadership pledge).

name: Alberta Auditor General Doug Wylie's request for a two-year extension to finish the health-procurement examination not granted; committee votes 5-4 to search for a successor (Nov 2025)
summary: Auditor General Doug Wylie, whose eight-year term ended April 28, 2026, asked the Standing Committee on Legislative Offices for a two-year extension so he could complete and report his examination of procurement at Alberta Health and AHS (CBC, Edmonton Journal). On Nov 3, 2025 UCP MLA Scott Cyr moved that the committee recommend a special committee to search for a new Auditor General; it carried 5-4 on a recorded vote (transcript). At the same meeting the committee also voted 5-4 to defer the Auditor General's supplementary funding request to December. Cyr said Wylie could reapply. The committee later recommended Phillip D. Peters, effective April 29, 2026 (committee report). Stopped (as reported): Committee motion (Cyr) to recommend a special search committee for a new Auditor General carried 5-4; Assembly passed Government Motion 13 on Nov 25, 2025; Phillip D. Peters recommended March 25, 2026 (by: Standing Committee on Legislative Offices (UCP majority)).

name: Alberta Chief Electoral Officer Glen Resler not reappointed; office vacant and run by acting officers May-Nov 2024
summary: On Nov 7, 2023 the Legislative Offices committee recommended a search for a new Chief Electoral Officer rather than reappointing Glen Resler, whose contract ran to May 2024 (transcript; the Globe reported the motion carried without opposition). The committee's June 2024 report says 'the position of Chief Electoral Officer is currently vacant'; with the deputy resigning, it recommended LaRae Petrowsky as Acting Chief Electoral Officer from July 4, 2024. The search committee recommended Gordon McClure in October 2024. Stopped (as reported): Office vacant after May 2024; acting appointment recommended June 20, 2024; permanent successor recommended October 2024 (by: Standing Committee on Legislative Offices; Select Special Ethics Commissioner and Chief Electoral Officer Search Committee).

name: Auditor General's DynaLIFE examination limited in scope: AHS, backed by the Health department, claimed legal and Cabinet privilege, redacted documents and destroyed the ex-CEO's notebooks (Nov 2025)
summary: The Auditor General Act gives the Auditor General access to information (s.14) and the power to compel evidence under oath (s.14.1). In 'An Examination of Community Laboratory Services (Contract with DynaLIFE)', released Nov 19, 2025, the Auditor General reported that AHS restricted access, 'supported by the Department of Health'. AHS claimed legal and Cabinet privilege over a wide range of documents, sometimes without clear rationale, ran a line-by-line lawyer review of more than 10,000 documents, and redacted large sections of thousands of them. Records were missing, password-locked or destroyed, including the former CEO's notebooks, 'despite our request to preserve evidence'. The office declared a scope limitation of indeterminate effect. Global reported 1,200 documents were fully redacted. Stopped (as reported): Privilege claims, redactions and destroyed/missing records caused a declared scope limitation (by: Alberta Health Services, supported by the Department of Health (per the Auditor General)).

name: Elections Alberta's 2025-26 supplementary funding request cut from $13.5M to $1.46M by Legislative Offices committee (Nov 2025)
summary: The Office of the Chief Electoral Officer asked for $13,512,118 in 2025-26 supplementary funding, including referendum preparation, recall petitions and citizen-initiative verification. UCP MLA Nolan Dyck moved to amend the request to $1,461,710; the motion carried 5-4 on a recorded vote (transcript). Dyck said much of the referendum cost was 12-18 months out and belonged in the spring budget; NDP members said it would slow processes the government had legislated. Stopped (as reported): Dyck amendment reducing the request to $1,461,710 carried 5-4 (by: Standing Committee on Legislative Offices (UCP majority)).

name: Alberta Assembly sets aside the independent Electoral Boundaries Commission's final map and hands redistribution to an MLA committee (Government Motion 37, Apr 2026)
summary: The Electoral Boundaries Commission, chaired by retired judge Dallas Miller, tabled an 89-seat final report on March 26, 2026, with a majority report, an addendum by the chair recommending 91 seats, and a minority report. Government House Leader Joseph Schow's Government Motion 37 urged a bill for 91 divisions and set up a Select Special Committee on Electoral Boundaries, chaired by Brandon Lunty, to oversee an advisory panel. A time-allocation motion (GM 39) passed 46-35, and GM 37 passed 44-36 on April 21, 2026 (Votes and Proceedings). CBC reported the motion rejects the commission's proposed boundaries and that the new MLA committee would not hold public hearings on a new map. Stopped (as reported): Government Motion 37 agreed 44-36 after time allocation (GM 39, 46-35); redistribution moved to a 5-member MLA committee and a 91-seat process (by: Legislative Assembly (government majority)).

name: Alberta Ethics Commissioner Marguerite Trussler not reappointed; committee opts for open search six months after her report on the Premier (Nov 2023)
summary: On May 17, 2023 Ethics Commissioner Marguerite Trussler found that Premier Danielle Smith contravened s.3 of the Conflicts of Interest Act in her interaction with the Justice Minister about a criminal case. On Nov 7, 2023, after an in-camera session on officer contracts, UCP MLA Glenn van Dijken moved that the Standing Committee on Legislative Offices recommend a select special committee to search for a new Ethics Commissioner; it passed on a voice vote. NDP MLA Marie Renaud spoke against it and said she had been ready to move Trussler's reappointment (transcript). Her contract expired in May 2024 (Globe and Mail). Stopped (as reported): Van Dijken motion recommending a select special committee to search for an Ethics Commissioner passed; Renaud's reappointment motion was not taken up because it was superseded (by: Standing Committee on Legislative Offices (UCP majority)).

name: Alberta Ethics Commissioner suspends investigation into MLAs accepting NHL hockey tickets under s.25(6) (active law-enforcement investigation) (Oct 2026)
summary: Speaker Ric McIver wrote on Oct 14, 2026 asking about the status of the Ethics Commissioner's investigation into MLAs accepting hockey tickets, noting s.24(6) bars the Assembly from inquiring into a matter referred to the Commissioner. In an Oct 20 reply, Ethics Commissioner Shawn McLeod said the investigation referenced in Feb 4, 2025 correspondence was suspended under s.25(6) (Edmonton Journal). The Commissioner's 2026 bulletin says s.25(6) requires suspension when the subject matter is also under law-enforcement investigation, and the investigation may resume once that is disposed of. The Journal said it was unclear whether this was linked to the RCMP's health-procurement investigation. Stopped (as reported): Investigation suspended under s.25(6) of the Conflicts of Interest Act (by: Ethics Commissioner of Alberta (statutory suspension)).

name: Alberta Office of the Seniors Advocate eliminated and consolidated into the Office of the Alberta Health Advocates (Budget 2019, effective Jan 2, 2020)
summary: The Office of the Seniors Advocate resolved individual seniors' issues and made systemic recommendations to the Minister. The Seniors and Housing 2019-20 Annual Report says that 'as part of Budget 2019, the OSA was consolidated with the Office of the Alberta Health Advocates under the Ministry of Health', which took over its responsibilities on Jan 2, 2020. Reporting said Seniors Advocate Dr. Sheree Kwong See's appointment ended Dec 31, 2019. Critics said non-health issues such as housing and income lost a dedicated advocate (Edmonton Journal; National Association of Federal Retirees). Stopped (as reported): OSA consolidated into the Health Advocate under Budget 2019; Health Advocates assumed its responsibilities Jan 2, 2020 (by: Government of Alberta (UCP), Minister of Seniors and Housing Josephine Pon).

name: BC Supreme Court refuses the Auditor General access to privileged records behind the $6M Basi-Virk legal-fee indemnity, limiting his audit (Jan 2013)
summary: In October 2010, former ministerial aides Dave Basi and Bobby Virk pleaded guilty in the BC Rail corruption case, and the government announced it had paid about $6 million in their legal fees. The Opposition demanded a public inquiry, which was not held. Auditor General John Doyle asked the court for the documents. Justice Robert Bauman dismissed the application, finding it a sweeping invasion of solicitor-client privilege (Times Colonist, Jan 30 2013). The OAG's December 2013 audit of special indemnities states that solicitor-client privilege prevents the Office from auditing the legal bills, and asks for that barrier to be addressed. Stopped (as reported): Court dismissed the AG's application; privilege bars audit of the legal bills (by: BC Supreme Court (Bauman J.), on solicitor-client privilege grounds).

name: BC legislative committee declines to give Auditor General John Doyle a second term, advertises the post, then under pressure offers only a two-year extension (Jan 2013)
summary: Auditor General John Doyle had criticized the BC Liberal government on issues including access to Basi-Virk documents and BC Hydro deferral accounts. He sought a second six-year term. Reappointment needed a unanimous recommendation from the five-member special committee (3 Liberal, 2 NDP). In early January 2013 the committee advertised for a new auditor general, which signalled the reappointment had been refused. NDP caucus chair Shane Simpson blamed the Liberal members. On January 23, 2013, after Premier Christy Clark publicly asked MLAs to reconsider, the committee unanimously offered Doyle a two-year extension instead of a full term (Times Colonist). Clark said legislation would move future auditors general to a single eight-year term. Stopped (as reported): Committee refused reappointment and began an external search; it then offered a two-year extension only (by: Special Committee to Appoint an Auditor General (BC Legislative Assembly; Liberal majority)).

name: BC defunds and closes the Auditor General for Local Government a year after an independent review said it offered value; the Act is repealed in 2022
summary: On February 7, 2019 the province said the AGLG would continue to operate after an independent review concluded it offered value. The February 2020 budget cut its funding by 31 per cent, from $2.6M to $1.8M. Municipal Affairs Minister Selina Robinson said the office would be phased out and that she would work with UBCM, which had long opposed it (Vancouver Sun). The office stopped operations in March 2021 (BC Government), and the Auditor General for Local Government Act was repealed effective June 2, 2022 (SBC 2022, c. 15, s. 1). Stopped (as reported): Funding cut and phase-out announced; operations ceased March 2021; Act repealed June 2, 2022 (by: Minister of Municipal Affairs and Housing Selina Robinson; Legislative Assembly (repeal)).

name: BC Liberal majority on the Finance committee votes 5-4 to refer the 2012 Health Ministry firings to the Ombudsperson rather than call the public inquiry sought by the fired researchers and the NDP (July 2015)
summary: In 2012 the Ministry of Health fired several drug-research employees and announced an RCMP referral. The researchers and the Opposition NDP called for a public inquiry. On July 29, 2015 the all-party committee instead voted 5-4, on party lines, to refer the matter to Ombudsperson Jay Chalke, after legislation was amended to strengthen his powers. Chalke had asked for a unanimous approach (CBC). The Ombudsperson's 2017 report, Misfire, found the investigation flawed and the dismissals unjustified, and government accepted its recommendations. Stopped (as reported): Committee referral to the Ombudsperson passed 5-4; no public inquiry called (by: Select Standing Committee on Finance and Government Services (Liberal majority)).

name: Clean Energy Act exempts the Site C dam and other BC Hydro projects from BC Utilities Commission certificate review (2010)
summary: Under the Utilities Commission Act, major utility projects need a Certificate of Public Convenience and Necessity from the BCUC (ss. 45-47), and energy supply contracts are reviewed under s. 71. Bill 17, the Clean Energy Act, was introduced in April 2010 by Energy Minister Blair Lekstrom. Section 7(1) exempts BC Hydro from those sections for listed projects, including (d) Site C, the third Peace River dam, and s. 7(3) bars the commission from acting to prevent the projects. NDP energy critic John Horgan said the exempted projects would not have appropriate oversight (CBC). The 2017 BCUC inquiry into Site C was an advisory review requested by government, not a certificate proceeding. Stopped (as reported): Statutory exemption, Clean Energy Act s. 7(1)(d) and s. 7(3) (by: BC Liberal government (Minister of Energy, Mines and Petroleum Resources), Legislative Assembly).

name: Nine of ten Manitoba Hydro-Electric Board members resign after the Premier blocks a Hydro-Manitoba Métis Federation agreement and declines to meet the board (Mar 21, 2018)
summary: On March 21, 2018 chair H. Sanford Riley and eight directors wrote to Crown Services Minister Cliff Cullen and resigned effective immediately. They said that for over a year they had tried to meet the Premier on critical finance and governance issues, including Hydro's relationship with Indigenous communities (Manitoba Hydro statement). Premier Brian Pallister said the trigger was the government's refusal to approve a payment of about $70 million to the Manitoba Métis Federation connected to the Manitoba-Minnesota transmission line, which he called 'persuasion money'. Riley called that characterization 'cynical, offensive and wrong' and said the agreement had been carefully vetted (CBC). Only PC MLA Cliff Graydon remained on the board. Stopped (as reported): Government declined to approve the MMF payment; board resigned en masse (by: Premier Brian Pallister / Government of Manitoba).

name: New Brunswick ends the stand-alone Right to Information and Privacy Commissioner, folding its role into a new Integrity Commissioner (Act Dec 2016, effective Sept 1, 2017)
summary: The Integrity Commissioner Act received royal assent on December 16, 2016. It deemed the Conflict of Interest Commissioner, Alexandre Deschênes, the first Integrity Commissioner. From September 1, 2017 it transferred to him the rights and responsibilities of the Right to Information and Protection of Privacy Commissioner, ending that stand-alone office (Integrity Commissioner annual report). Before this, the conflict-of-interest post had been filled on an interim basis for a year by Anne Bertrand, the privacy commissioner, after Alfred Landry retired on July 31, 2015. In 2019 the access and privacy oversight was moved again, to the Ombud (per search; not verified). Stopped (as reported): Integrity Commissioner Act: privacy commissioner functions transferred; stand-alone office ended (by: Government of New Brunswick (Liberal); Legislative Assembly).

name: Newfoundland and Labrador Bill 29 removes the Information and Privacy Commissioner's power to review refusals based on official Cabinet records and solicitor-client privilege (June 2012)
summary: Bill 29, An Act to Amend the Access to Information and Protection of Privacy Act, was introduced on June 11, 2012 by Justice Minister Felix Collins after the Cummings statutory review. It broadened the definition of Cabinet records (NL release). The OIPC's 2012-13 annual report states that Bill 29 removed the Commissioner's authority to review refusals based on solicitor-client privilege (s. 21) or official Cabinet record claims (s. 18(2)(a)), and that he could no longer demand those records; applicants had to go to the Trial Division instead. The bill passed after a filibuster of about 70 hours (June 11-14) and came into force June 27, 2012 (OIPC). The 2014-15 independent ATIPPA review led to a replacement Act in 2015. Stopped (as reported): Bill 29 amendments in force (by: Government of Newfoundland and Labrador (PC); House of Assembly).

name: Ontario's first Chief Scientist, Molly Shoichet, dismissed and the position's orders in council revoked; no successor named (June-July 2018)
summary: The position of Special Advisor, Chief Scientist was created by O.C. 2242/2017, and Molly Shoichet was appointed by O.C. 2243/2017 (Nov 17, 2017). Her remuneration O.C. 2461/2017 shows it was 'Revoked by: Order in Council 988/2018', a Premier's order of June 29, 2018 revoking a list of orders. On July 3-5, 2018 Shoichet was told she was let go. The Premier's spokesperson said the government would find a 'suitable and qualified replacement' (CBC), but no successor appointment was found. Stopped (as reported): O.C. 988/2018 revoked the orders; Chief Scientist dismissed (by: Premier and President of the Council (O.C. 988/2018)).

name: Ontario Bill 97 retroactively removes records of the Premier, ministers and their staff from FOI law, taking the Premier's personal-device use outside the Privacy Commissioner's authority (Apr 2026)
summary: Opposition Leader Marit Stiles asked the Information and Privacy Commissioner to investigate the Premier's use of personal devices for government business. On April 27, 2026 the IPC replied that once the Bill 97 amendments (Plan to Protect Ontario Act (Budget Measures), 2026) come into force, records held by the Premier, cabinet ministers, parliamentary assistants and their staff are excluded from FIPPA, retroactive to 1988, and fall outside the IPC's statutory authority to investigate (IPC). CBC/Canadian Press reported that Premier Doug Ford said part of the rationale was to stop a Global News request for his cellphone records. The government skipped committee hearings, and the bill passed 57-33 on April 23, 2026. Stopped (as reported): Bill 97 enacted; exclusion retroactive to January 1, 1988; IPC states the records are outside its authority to investigate (by: Government of Ontario (PC majority), Legislative Assembly of Ontario).

name: Hydro One's entire board resigns and CEO Mayo Schmidt retires under agreement with the new Ontario government; Hydro One Accountability Act passed (July-Aug 2018)
summary: On July 11, 2018 Energy Minister Greg Rickford accepted a letter of agreement from Hydro One chair David Denison. The entire board would resign and be replaced on or before August 15, 2018, CEO Mayo Schmidt would retire that day with a $400,000 lump sum and no severance, and CFO Paul Dobson would be acting CEO (Ontario Newsroom). The Hydro One Accountability Act, 2018 then required a new executive compensation framework subject to provincial approval. The board's terms were cut short through the province's shareholder leverage (it held a minority stake) after a PC campaign pledge. Stopped (as reported): Board resignations and replacement by Aug 15, 2018; CEO retirement; statute imposing compensation controls (by: Minister of Energy Greg Rickford (Government of Ontario), by agreement with the board).

name: Ontario Ombudsman twice declines to review the OPP commissioner hiring (Taverner); the deputy commissioner who sought the review, Brad Blair, is fired (Dec 2018-Mar 2019)
summary: In December 2018 OPP deputy commissioner Brad Blair asked Ombudsman Paul Dubé to review the hiring process that chose Toronto police Supt. Ron Taverner, a longtime friend of Premier Doug Ford, as OPP commissioner. Dubé twice declined, on the basis that the appointment was ultimately a cabinet decision outside his jurisdiction. Blair applied to the Divisional Court (Blair v. The Ombudsman of Ontario, 2019 ONSC 369; an expedited hearing was denied). On March 4, 2019 Blair was fired. Minister Sylvia Jones said he had released confidential OPP information; the termination was recommended by Deputy Minister Mario Di Tommaso, who sat on the hiring panel, and approved by the Public Service Commission (CBC). Taverner later withdrew. Stopped (as reported): Ombudsman declined jurisdiction (twice); court application not expedited; requester dismissed by revocation of appointment (by: Ontario Ombudsman (declined); Deputy Minister / Public Service Commission and cabinet (dismissal)).

name: Quebec's 2016-17 budget ends the independent Commissaire à la santé et au bien-être (health system performance watchdog); the post sits inactive until revived in 2019
summary: The Commissaire à la santé et au bien-être (CSBE) was created in 2005-06 to independently evaluate the performance of Quebec's health and social services system. Its commissioner since 2006 was Robert Salois. The office's 2016-17 annual report records that the cessation of its activities was announced on March 16, 2016, in the 2016-17 budget. Salois said he learned of it from a civil servant without explanation (Radio-Canada/CP). Health Minister Gaétan Barrette said its functions overlapped with other bodies and that the move made economic sense (CBC). In March 2019 the CAQ government's Health Minister Danielle McCann said the post, then 'inactive', would be re-established (Radio-Canada). Stopped (as reported): Budget 2016-17 announced cessation of the CSBE's activities; most staff departed (by: Government of Quebec (Couillard, Liberal); Minister of Health Gaétan Barrette).

name: Quebec's Bill 39 (mixed-member proportional voting system with a 2022 referendum) passes second reading 93-28, then is dropped; no referendum held (2019-2021)
summary: The CAQ had committed in 2018 to reform the voting system (Radio-Canada). Minister Sonia LeBel tabled Bill 39, Loi établissant un nouveau mode de scrutin, on September 25, 2019. It proposed a mixed system with a regional proportional component and a referendum at the 2022 election. The Commission des institutions held consultations in January and February 2020, and the principle was adopted on October 8, 2020 by 93 to 28 (Assemblée nationale). On April 28, 2021 LeBel said there was not enough time to pass the 290-clause bill before a 2022 referendum. In December 2021 Premier François Legault said the government would not call the bill again (Journal de Québec). Detailed study never concluded. Stopped (as reported): Government declared no referendum in 2022 and abandoned the bill; it was never passed (by: Government of Quebec (CAQ): Premier François Legault, Minister Sonia LeBel).

name: Saskatchewan government declines an NDP call for a judicial inquiry into Global Transportation Hub land purchases, and PAC defeats a motion to question officials (Mar-Nov 2016)
summary: In March 2016 NDP Leader Cam Broten called for a judicial inquiry into GTH/Regina Bypass land purchases. He cited a Ministry of Highways appraisal far below the price paid. The government declined, and Cabinet instead asked the Provincial Auditor (Feb 9, 2016) to examine whether proper procedures were followed and appropriate value received. The Auditor's report found the GTH paid too much. On November 8, 2016 at the Public Accounts Committee, NDP member Cathy Sproule moved to have deputy economy minister Laurie Pushor and the current and former GTH CEOs appear. The motion was defeated. Premier Brad Wall said the four individuals had already been questioned in the audit (Global News/CP). Police investigated; this pass did not check whether that led to charges. Stopped (as reported): No judicial inquiry called; PAC witness motion defeated (by: Government of Saskatchewan (Saskatchewan Party); government members of PAC).

name: Saskatchewan Public Accounts Committee defeats NDP motion asking the Provincial Auditor to investigate the Global Transportation Hub's attempt to land a Costco store (May 13, 2025)
summary: Costco, which had planned a Regina store at Westerra, had been in talks about locating at the provincial Global Transportation Hub (GTH). Regina council then approved an incentive package of almost $7 million to keep it at Westerra (620 CKRM). On May 13, 2025 NDP MLA Hugh Gordon moved that the Public Accounts Committee, under s. 16(1) of The Provincial Auditor Act, ask the Provincial Auditor to perform a special assignment investigating the GTH's actions, procedures, policies and expenditures in the attempted deal. The motion was defeated on a voice vote; the Chair declared that 'the nos have it' (PAC Hansard). GTH minister David Marit did not take media questions, and GTH CEO Daniel Hersche said Costco's agent had approached GTH's broker (620 CKRM). name: House order to 'collect and recoup' ArriveCAN funds within 100 days not met by the deadline (motion adopted Feb 28, 2024)
summary: Per Journals No. 287, the House adopted (170–149, Division No. 648) the opposition motion of Mr. Poilievre, seconded by Mr. Nater, including part '(b) call on the government to collect and recoup all funds paid to ArriveCAN contractors and subcontractors which did no work on the ArriveCAN app, within 100 days of this motion being adopted, and for the Prime Minister to table a report in the House demonstrating that taxpayer funds have been repaid.' At OGGO meeting 132 (Jul 23, 2024, block (1250)), Larry Brock said: 'One hundred days from February 28 would have been June 6. ... Nothing but crickets.' In an answer to Q-3138 (Hansard No. 389, Dec 13, 2024), Jennifer O’Connell said 'the CBSA is currently reviewing all invoices submitted by GC Strategies, Coradix Technology Consulting and Dalian Enterprises Inc. to determine whether any overpayments were issued'. What stopped it: Attributed only: Brock (OGGO 132, (1250)): 'One hundred days from February 28 would have been June 6. That passed over a month ago. ... Nothing but crickets.' O’Connell (Q-3138): 'the CBSA is currently reviewing all invoices submitted by GC Strategies, Coradix Technology Consulting and Dalian Enterprises Inc. to determine whether any overpayments were issued'.

name: Canada's commercial-spyware pledges (2023 Joint Statement, 2024 Pall Mall) not implemented domestically (as of 2026)
summary: Canada endorsed the March 30, 2023 Joint Statement on Efforts to Counter the Proliferation and Misuse of Commercial Spyware (listed again in the September 22, 2024 update), which commits signatories to guardrails on government spyware use and to preventing exports to likely malicious end-users. Canada is also listed among 'States and international organisations represented' at the Pall Mall Process declaration (Lancaster House, 6 February 2024). Canada is not among the 'Supporting States' of the Pall Mall Process Code of Practice for States (GOV.UK page updated 23 October 2025, retrieved 2026-10-29). On March 23, 2026, Citizen Lab director Ronald Deibert told SDIR that Canada has not put in place export controls or restrictions on mercenary surveillance vendors and has 'done almost nothing' to live up to its pledge. No official federal follow-up (spyware-specific export control, procurement ban or vendor list) was located. Distinct from the existing 2023 ban-list non-event (ETHI Rec 2, government response 2023-03-23). What stopped it: As of March 23, 2026, testimony to Parliament states Canada has no export controls or restrictions on mercenary surveillance vendors and has done almost nothing on the pledge; Canada is not listed as a supporting State of the Pall Mall Code of Practice. No government explanation located.

name: Government did not commit to a Criminal Code Part VI review after ETHI Report 7 (2023)
summary: ETHI Report 7 Rec 3 called for a review of Criminal Code Part VI (invasion of privacy / interception) in light of ODITs. The government response did not commit to a review and said it was 'receptive to further potential reforms'. What stopped it: No review was committed in the response.

name: CSIS kept dataset information the CSIS Act required destroyed from July 2019 (NSIRA review 21-15)
summary: The CSIS Act dataset regime (from the National Security Act, 2017; in force July 2019) requires datasets not meeting the regime to be destroyed. NSIRA found that 'as of August 2023, CSIS did not comply with the dataset provisions in the CSIS Act' because it retained Canadian information extracted from foreign datasets that 'should have been destroyed upon coming into force of the NSA 2017, in July, 2019', and that CSIS had not exhaustively scanned its systems. What stopped it: Per NSIRA, CSIS retained the information and had not exhaustively scanned its systems as of Aug 2023. CSIS's response says the records were kept 'to meet a corporate record keeping obligation' and later destroyed, and rejects the exhaustive scan as 'not feasible' (response PDF pp.4-5).

name: CSIS rejects NSIRA 21-15 recommendations to destroy retained information and scan its systems (2024)
summary: NSIRA review 21-15 recommended that CSIS immediately destroy names retained from exigent-circumstances queries (R2), immediately destroy a case study dataset collected under s.12 (R12), and conduct an exhaustive scan of its repositories to destroy non-compliant information (R8). The government response marks all three 'Disagree'. On R2 and R12 CSIS states 'NSIRA's interpretation of 'strictly necessary' is overly narrow such that it would unreasonably impede CSIS' ability to meet its mandates' (pp.2, 6); on R8 it says an exhaustive search 'is not feasible' (p.5). CSIS also disagreed with R6 (cease duplicating information). What stopped it: CSIS disagreed with Recommendations 2, 8 and 12 in the published government response.

name: ETHI never voted on the Hepfner motion on RCMP use of Pegasus/NSO tools (2022)

Debate arose; MP Matthew Green moved to adjourn; the vote was 5-5 and the presiding Chair voted in favour, so the committee adjourned without voting on the motion. What stopped it: Adjournment motion carried on the Chair's deciding vote.

Parliament was prorogued Jan 6, 2025 (SI/2025-9); the study page lists no government response. What stopped it: Prorogation on Jan 6, 2025 ended the session before the response deadline; no response is listed.

name: No federal moratorium on police facial recognition after ETHI Report 6
summary: ETHI Report 6 Rec 18 called for a federal moratorium on facial recognition by federal police and industry unless done with OPC consultation or judicial authorization. The government response 'acknowledges' it, says the Privacy Act already governs federal institutions, and points to Privacy Act modernization and the proposed CPPA (Bill C-27); no moratorium is committed. What stopped it: The response acknowledged the recommendation without imposing a moratorium.

name: No independent advisory body on police surveillance technology after ETHI Report 7 (2023)
summary: ETHI Report 7 Rec 8 called for an independent advisory body to set national standards on new technology used by police. The government response pointed instead to the RCMP's internal National Technology Onboarding Program (NTOP). What stopped it: The response substituted the RCMP-internal NTOP for an independent body.

name: ETHI Report 7 Privacy Act reforms (mandatory PIAs, OPC order powers) not implemented
summary: ETHI Report 7 (Nov 2022) recommended Privacy Act changes after the RCMP ODIT study: mandatory PIAs submitted to the OPC (Rec 1), privacy as a fundamental right (Rec 4), OPC order-making powers (Rec 6), privacy by design (Rec 7), and transparency (Rec 9). The government response (Mar 2023) said it was 'considering elevating to legislation' the PIA requirement and pointed to Justice's 2020 discussion paper and Bill C-27. The OPC told the Senate on Oct 14, 2025 that 'The Privacy Act... has remained unchanged since 1983', and its 2024-25 annual report says Bill C-27 'died on the order paper with the prorogation of Parliament in January 2025' and calls for 'long-awaited reform of the Privacy Act'. ETHI Report 13 (2024) repeated five of these recommendations. What stopped it: The government only committed to consider; per the OPC, the Privacy Act remained unchanged as of Oct 2025, and Bill C-27 (covering the PIPEDA side) died on prorogation.

name: RCMP did not agree to OPC recommendations on Project Wide Awake (2024)
summary: After MP Charlie Angus's 2020 complaint, the OPC recommended the RCMP stop collecting personal information from login-protected sources via Babel X and fix its public transparency (s.11 personal information bank descriptions). 'The RCMP did not agree to implement the recommendation, and therefore, we consider this matter to not be resolved.' The transparency issue was found 'well-founded and not resolved', and the RCMP did not commit to implementing its own PIA's recommendations within 12 months. What stopped it: The RCMP refused the OPC recommendation on Babel X login-protected sources and did not resolve the transparency finding.

name: RCMP privacy impact assessment for device investigative tools delayed until 2023
summary: Per ETHI Report 7, the RCMP had used ODITs since at least 2017 (CAIT established 2016 per Q-566) and began drafting a PIA only in 2021; D/Commr. Bryan Larkin confirmed in Aug 2022 that no PIA had been completed, and the OPC said it was not consulted. Per OPC issue sheets, the OPC received the PIA on Sept 12, 2023, gave advice in Dec 2023, and found it 'conducted at a very high level which made it difficult to assess privacy risks.' What stopped it: The PIA was not complete at the Aug 2022 hearing and reached the OPC only on Sept 12, 2023.

name: Government declined to create a banned spyware vendor list after ETHI Report 7 (2023)
summary: ETHI Report 7 Rec 2 called for a list of banned spyware vendors and export-control rules. At meeting 33 Ronald Deibert (Citizen Lab) said 'there really are zero licensing or export controls in this country for the export or sale of spyware'. The government response did not create a banned-vendor list; it pointed to the existing Export Control List, the Export and Import Permits Act and the Export Controls and Human Rights Initiative. What stopped it: The government response declined to create a list and referred to existing export-control instruments.
